name: House strategy

concepts.name: Trend following
concepts.idea: What has been rising for months tends to keep rising for a while, and the same for falling. Hold what is above its long average; step aside from what is below.

concepts.name: Risk parity
concepts.idea: Size positions so each brings the same risk. Bonds then get more money than shares. Funds borrow to lift the return; we do not.
concepts.evidence: Widely documented; the unborrowed version gives smaller swings and a lower return.

concepts.name: Volatility targeting
concepts.idea: Cut exposure when markets turn violent. Violent markets have not paid enough extra to justify staying fully in.

concepts.name: Value with a margin of safety
concepts.idea: Buy only well below your own estimate of what the business is worth.
concepts.ours: Scorecard check, using our own cash-flow valuation.

concepts.name: Momentum between shares
concepts.idea: Shares that beat the market over the past year (leaving out the latest month) tend to keep beating it for some months.

concepts.name: Quality
concepts.idea: Profitable, steady businesses have earned more than their risk suggests.
concepts.evidence: Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen (Quality minus junk).

concepts.name: Insider purchases
concepts.idea: Executives buying their own shares in the open market with their own money is informative; their sales say little.

concepts.name: Copying well-known investors
concepts.idea: Follow the large, slow positions of chosen long-term managers. The filings are up to 45 days late, so it only works for patient holders.
concepts.evidence: Mixed; works best for concentrated, low-turnover managers.
concepts.ours: Scorecard check, never a reason on its own.

concepts.name: Earnings drift
concepts.idea: After a clear earnings surprise the price tends to keep drifting the same way for weeks.

concepts.name: Hard risk limits per bet
concepts.idea: Every bet has a loss limit and a size cap; risk is cut after losses; many unrelated bets beat a few big ones.
concepts.evidence: Industry practice rather than a paper.
concepts.ours: Rule 6, the maximum-loss line, the position caps and the correlation table.

concepts.name: Long/short and market-neutral
concepts.idea: Own the best shares, sell short the worst, and earn the gap whatever the market does.
concepts.evidence: Works only with cheap borrowing and tight risk control.
concepts.ours: Needs short selling, which your broker and profile do not allow. The lowest scores are an avoid list instead.

concepts.name: Global macro
concepts.idea: Large views on interest rates, currencies and commodities, usually through futures.
concepts.evidence: Depends on the manager, not on a rule.
concepts.ours: The trend rule across asset classes is the systematic part. Judgement bets are left out.

concepts.name: Merger arbitrage
concepts.idea: Buy a company after a takeover is announced and earn the gap to the deal price. Small steady gains, a large loss when a deal breaks.
concepts.ours: Needs many deals at once to be safe. Could be added later as a watch list of announced deals.

concepts.name: Statistical arbitrage
concepts.idea: Thousands of tiny, short-lived price gaps traded with borrowed money at almost no cost.
concepts.evidence: The edge is in speed, scale and cost.
concepts.ours: Out of reach: our costs per trade are larger than the gaps.

concepts.name: Carry and selling volatility
concepts.idea: Collect a steady yield or option premium and accept a rare, sudden large loss.
concepts.ours: Needs derivatives and borrowing. The only carry we take is the yield on short Treasuries.

concepts.name: Tail hedging
concepts.idea: Pay a small regular cost for options that pay off hugely in a crash.
concepts.evidence: Costly in normal years by design.
concepts.ours: Needs options. Bonds, gold, the trend rule and the doomsday protocol stand in for it.

concepts.name: Sizing by edge (Kelly)
concepts.idea: Bet more when the edge is larger and the outcome surer; in practice only a fraction, because the edge is never known exactly.
concepts.evidence: Thorp's work on the Kelly criterion.
concepts.ours: Our sizing is the cautious relative: a fixed small loss per idea.

variants.name: S&P 500 fund, held
variants.what: All the money in US shares.

variants.name: 60% shares, 40% bonds
variants.what: The classic balanced mix, reset monthly.

variants.name: Equal money
variants.what: The four assets with the same money in each.

variants.name: Equal money + trend rule
variants.what: The four assets with the same money in each. Each is held only above its 200-day average.

variants.name: Equal risk
variants.what: The four assets with the same risk in each.

variants.name: Equal risk + trend rule
variants.what: The four assets with the same risk in each. Each is held only above its 200-day average.

variants.name: Equal risk, tilted to shares
variants.what: Equal risk, then 50% of the money moved towards the two share funds.

variants.name: Equal risk, tilted to shares + trend rule
variants.what: Equal risk, then 50% of the money moved towards the two share funds. Each is held only above its 200-day average.

robustness.what: The chosen rules re-run with nearby settings: the volatility window at 40, 60 or 120 days, and the cap, the trend window or the tilt a step lower and higher.

backtest.verdict: From 2005 to 2026 the house core made 7.0% a year against 11.2% for the S&P 500 fund and 8.3% for 60/40. Its worst fall was 19%, against 55% and 33%.

chosen.name: Equal risk
chosen.why: 4 of the 6 candidates kept their worst fall within 24%, which is 80% of the 30% maximum loss in your profile. Of those, this one made the most. Kept since go-live; the choice is made again only when your risk profile or the strategy version changes.
chosen.trend_note: The trend rule on this mix cut the worst fall from 19% to 11% and changed the yearly return from 7.0% to 5.3%. It is left out, because your maximum loss does not need it and it costs return.

backtest.income_note: The price files leave out dividends and bond interest, so an estimate is added back: 1.8% a year for US shares, 2.8% for shares outside the US, the 10-year Treasury yield for the bond fund and the 2-year yield for short Treasuries.
backtest.method: Daily prices from CNBC. Decisions at each month end, held to the next; every trade costs 0.25% of the amount moved. The test starts once all four assets and a year of history exist. Six candidate mixes are tested, all with the volatility cap; the one for your profile is picked by a rule fixed in advance, then re-run with nearby settings to show the result does not hang on one choice.
limits: A back-test is history, not a promise; these years include a long fall in interest rates that helped bonds for most of the period.
Picking the best of six candidates flatters the winner a little, even with a rule fixed in advance.
Dividend and interest income is an estimate, so every yearly figure can be off by a few tenths of a point.
US-listed funds stand in for the EU-listed ones you would buy; currency moves against the forint are not included.
The share scorecard cannot be back-tested, because past insider, holder and valuation data were not saved. It is tracked forward on paper from today.

rules.rule: Spread the core over four different things: US shares, shares outside the US, government bonds and gold.
rules.from: All-weather thinking: hold assets that do well in different climates (growth, recession, inflation).

rules.rule: Give each of the four the same share of the risk, not the same money: the calmer an asset has been over 60 days, the more of it.
rules.from: Risk parity, without the borrowing that funds add on top.

rules.rule: If the mix's estimated volatility is above 20% a year (the cap for your risk level), shrink everything in proportion and park the rest.
Single shares get at most 30% in total, and only those passing at least 5 of 7 checks, always including an upward trend.
rules.from: Value, quality, momentum, insider buying, well-known holders and earnings drift, used as one scorecard.

rules.rule: Size every share by the loss you accept if its stop is hit, never by conviction, and never above the one-company limit.
rules.from: Risk limits as multi-manager funds apply them to each bet.

rules.rule: Change the mix once a month, not in between, unless the doomsday protocol says otherwise.
rules.from: Low turnover: costs are the one certain number in any strategy.

rules_note: The trend rule on this mix cut the worst fall from 19% to 11% and changed the yearly return from 7.0% to 5.3%. It is left out, because your maximum loss does not need it and it costs return.
summary: A core of four asset classes (equal risk) with a volatility cap, plus up to 30% in single shares that pass a seven-point scorecard. It runs on paper: it changes no decision card until you switch it on.
